anchors.1: Related information is scattered with no discernible grouping; the reader must hunt across the whole page to assemble any one concept.
anchors.3: Basic grouping exists (e.g. issuer vs. customer are visually separate) but placement is inconsistent or some related fields are still split across distant regions.
anchors.4: Every field lives in one clearly bounded group matching the domain's natural structure, each in an expected location.
anchors.5: Grouping is clear AND the zones are ordered to match the reader's natural scanning path, so the reader never backtracks to find related information.

anchors.1: Every field has the same size/weight; no single fact stands out from the rest.
anchors.3: Some size/weight variation exists, but the one fact the reader needs first is not clearly the most prominent element on the page.
anchors.4: The one fact the reader needs first is visually dominant — larger and/or bolder than everything else.
anchors.5: The key fact is dominant AND every other element recedes in proportion to its importance, producing one unambiguous focal point.

anchors.1: The layout could be mistaken for a different kind of document entirely; it lacks the conventional elements a reader expects for this document type.
anchors.3: The document is recognizable as the right family but is missing one or more conventional elements a reader would expect.
anchors.4: The document includes and positions the conventional elements a reader of this domain expects.
anchors.5: The document is indistinguishable in structure and convention from a real-world professional document of this type.

anchors.1: No navigational aids exist — a wall of unlabeled text or numbers with no alignment or whitespace to guide scanning.
anchors.3: Some labels exist, but alignment or whitespace is inconsistent.
anchors.4: Labels, alignment, and whitespace are applied consistently throughout.
anchors.5: Affordances actively anticipate the reader's exact scanning path.

anchors.1: Type sizing/weight is arbitrary or inconsistent; text is cramped, overflowing, or wrapped awkwardly.
anchors.3: Sizing/weight is mostly consistent, but a few awkward line breaks or spacing issues remain.
anchors.4: Sizing, weight, and spacing are consistent throughout with no awkward breaks.
anchors.5: Every typographic choice reads as intentional — a coherent, deliberate type system with zero awkward breaks.

anchors.1: The document is visually noisy or internally inconsistent across sections.
anchors.3: The document is mostly restrained, but one or two decorative inconsistencies remain.
anchors.4: The document is fully restrained and internally consistent.
anchors.5: The document is restrained, consistent, AND every visual element earns its place — nothing could be removed without losing information.

gates.label: Reading order
gates.description: The rendered PDF's content reads top-to-bottom, left-to-right in the same order a human would naturally scan it, with no illogical jumps between regions. Pass/fail, no partial credit.

gates.label: Print safety
gates.description: The document renders correctly at its actual print/paper size: no clipped text or table columns at page margins, and no essential content lost or orphaned across a page break. Pass/fail, no partial credit.

stress_exemption.reason: Stress-matrix fixtures (test/rendro/edge_matrix_test.exs) exist to prove pipeline robustness and byte-determinism under adversarial inputs -- overflow, extreme text length, empty/60+ line-item counts, numeric edge cases, currency and page-size variance -- not reader-facing aesthetic quality. They are deliberately excluded from the reader-quality rubric's beauty gate; the gate applies only to curated family x domain demonstration documents.
